title: Herod’s plot and the kingdom not of this world
source_text: Εἰ δ᾿ Ἡρώδης ἐπεβούλευσε τῷ γεννηθέντι, κἂν μὴ πιστεύσῃ ἀληθῶς τοῦτο γεγονέναι ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος, οὐ θαυμαστόν. τυφλὸν γάρ τι ἐστὶν ἡ πονηρία καὶ βουλομένη ὡς ἰσχυροτέρα τοῦ χρεὼν νικᾶν αὐτό. ὅπερ καὶ Ἡρώδης παθὼν καὶ πεπίστευκε βασιλέα γεγεννῆσθαι Ἰουδαίων καὶ ἀνομολογουμένην εἶχε τῇ πίστει ταύτῃ συγκατάθεσιν, μὴ ἰδὼν ὅτι ἤτοι πάντως βασιλεύς ἐστι καὶ βασιλεύσει, ἢ οὐ βασιλεύσει καὶ μάτην ἀναιρεθήσεται. ἐβουλήθη οὖν αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι, μαχομένας διὰ τὴν κακίαν ἔχων κρίσεις ὑπὸ τοῦ τυφλοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ διαβόλου κινούμενος, ὃς καὶ ἀρχῆθεν ἐπεβούλευε τῷ σωτῆρι, φαντασθεὶς αὐτὸν εἶναί τινα μέγαν καὶ ἔσεσθαι. „ἄγγελος“ μὲν οὖν ἐχρημάτισε τῷ Ἰωσὴφ τὴν ἀκολουθίαν τῶν πραγμάτων τηρῶν, κἂν μὴ πιστεύῃ Κέλσος, ἀναχωρῆσαι μετὰ τοῦ παιδὸς καὶ τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ „εἰς Αἴγυπτον“ ὁ δ᾿ Ἡρώδης „ἀνεῖλε“ πάντα τὰ „ἐν Βηθλεὲμ“ καὶ „τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῆς“ παιδία, ὡς συναναιρήσων τὸν γεννηθέντα Ἰουδαίων βασιλέα. οὐγὰρ ἑώρα τὴν ἀκοίμητον φρουρὸν δύναμιν τῶν ἀξίων φρουρεῖσθαι καὶ τηρεῖσθαι τῇ σωτηρίᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὧν πρῶτος πάντων τιμῇ καὶ ὑπεροχῇ πάσῃ μείζων ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, βασιλεὺς, οὐχ ὡς Ἡρώδης ᾤετο, ἐσόμενος, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ἔπρεπε τὸν θεὸν διδόναι βασιλείαν ἐπ᾿ εὐεργεσίᾳ τῶν βασιλευομένων τῷ οὐ μέσην καὶ ἀδιάφορον, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, εὐεργεσίαν εὐεργετήσοντι τοὺς ὑποτεταγμένους ἀλλὰ νόμοις ἀληθῶς θεοῦ παιδεύσοντι καὶ ὑπάξοντι αὐτούς· ὅπερ καὶ Ἰησοῦς ἐπιστάμενος καὶ ἀρνούμενος μὲν τὸ εἶναι, ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ ἐκδέχονται, βασιλεὺς διδάσκων δὲ τὸ ἐξαίρετον τῆς ἑαυτοῦ βασιλείας φησὶ τό· „εἰ ἦν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμὴ, οἱ ὑπηρέται οἱ ἐμοὶ ἠγωνίζοντο ἂν, ἵνα μὴ παραδοθῶ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις· νυνὶ δὲ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμή.“ ταῦτα δ᾿ εἰ ἑωράκει ὁ Κέλσος, οὐκ ἂν ἔλεγεν· εἰ δ᾿ ὅπως μὴ σὺ αὐξηθεὶς ἀντ᾿ ἐκείνου βασιλεύῃς, τί ἐπειδή γε ηὐξήθης, οὐ βασιλεύεις, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς οὕτως ἀγεννῶς ἀγείρεις κυπτάζων ὑπὸ φόβου καὶ περιφθειρόμενος ἄνω κάτω; οὐκ ἔστι δ᾿ ἀγεννὲς τὸ μετ᾿ οἰκονομίας περιϊστάμενον τοὺς κινδύνους μὴ ὁμόσε αὐτοῖς χωρεῖν, οὐ διὰ φόβον θανάτου ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὲρ τοῦ χρησίμως αὐτὸν τῷ βίῳ ἐπιδημοῦντα ἑτέρους ὠφελεῖν, ἕως ἐπιστῇ ὁ ἐπιτήδειος καιρὸς τοῦ τὸν ἀνειληφότα ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν ἀνθρώπου θάνατον ἀποθανεῖν, ἔχοντά τι χρήσιμον τοῖς ἀνθρώποις· ὅπερ δῆλόν ἐστι τῷ νοήσαντι τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων ἀποθανεῖν· περὶ οὗ κατὰ δύναμιν ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων εἴπομεν.
pass_a_gloss: If Herod plotted (ἐπεβούλευσε) against the one born, even if the Jew in Celsus does not believe this truly happened, [it is] not wonderful. For wickedness (πονηρία) is something blind (τυφλόν), and wishing, as stronger than what must be (τοῦ χρεών), to conquer it. Which Herod too suffering, both believed (πεπίστευκε) a king of the Jews to have been born and had an assent (συγκατάθεσιν) not agreeing (ἀνομολογουμένην) with this belief (πίστει), not seeing that either he is altogether (πάντως) king and will reign, or he will not reign and will be killed in vain (μάτην). He wished then to kill him, having judgements (κρίσεις) fighting [each other] through vice (κακίαν), moved by the blind and wicked devil (διαβόλου), who also from the beginning (ἀρχῆθεν) plotted against the Saviour, imagining (φαντασθείς) him to be someone great and to be going to be. An 'angel' then warned (ἐχρημάτισε) Joseph, keeping (τηρῶν) the sequence (ἀκολουθίαν) of events, even if Celsus does not believe, to withdraw with the child and his mother 'into Egypt'; and Herod 'killed' all the children 'in Bethlehem' and 'its borders (ὁρίοις)', as going to kill together the born king of the Jews. For he did not see the sleepless (ἀκοίμητον) guarding power (φρουρὸν δύναμιν) of those worthy to be guarded and kept for the salvation (σωτηρίᾳ) of men, of whom first of all, greater in honour and all pre-eminence (ὑπεροχῇ), was Jesus, going to be king, not as Herod thought, but as it was fitting for God to give a kingdom for benefit (εὐεργεσίᾳ) of the ruled to one who would benefit the subjects with a benefit not middling and indifferent (ἀδιάφορον), that I may so name it, but would educate (παιδεύσοντι) and bring them under (ὑπάξοντι) laws truly of God; which Jesus also knowing, and denying (ἀρνούμενος) being king as the many take it (ἐκδέχονται), but teaching the distinctiveness (τὸ ἐξαίρετον) of his own kingdom, says: 'If my kingdom were of this world, my servants (ὑπηρέται) would be fighting, that I not be handed over to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not of this world.' If Celsus had seen these things he would not say: 'If so that you, having grown, might not reign instead of him, why, since you have grown, do you not reign, but you the child/son of God (ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς) so ignobly (ἀγεννῶς) beg/collect (ἀγείρεις), stooping (κυπτάζων) from fear and wandering wretchedly (περιφθειρόμενος) up and down?' It is not ignoble, with economy/purpose (μετ᾿ οἰκονομίας), going around (περιϊστάμενον) dangers, not to go to meet them, not through fear of death but in order that, sojourning usefully in life, he might benefit others, until the fitting time (ἐπιτήδειος καιρός) arrived for the one who had taken up human nature (ἀνειληφότα ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν) to die a man's death, having something useful for men; which is clear to him who has understood Jesus to have died for (ὑπέρ) men; about which according to [our] power we spoke in the [books/sections] before these.
pass_b_english: If Herod plotted against the newborn child, it is no wonder, even if Celsus's Jew does not believe that this really happened. For wickedness is a blind thing, and wants to defeat what is destined, as though it were stronger. This is what happened to Herod too. He believed that a king of the Jews had been born, and yet he held a conviction at odds with that belief, not seeing that either the child was certainly a king and would reign, or he would not reign and to kill him would be pointless. So he wanted to kill him, his judgements set at war with one another by his wickedness, moved by the blind and wicked devil, who from the beginning plotted against the Saviour, imagining him to be someone great and to be destined for greatness.

An “angel,” then, preserving the order of events, warned Joseph, even if Celsus does not believe it, to withdraw with the child and his mother “into Egypt” (Matthew 2:13); and Herod “killed” all the children “in Bethlehem” and “in its region” (Matthew 2:16), thinking to kill along with them the king of the Jews who had been born. For he did not see the sleepless power that guards those who are worthy to be guarded and kept safe for the salvation of human beings. Of these the first of all, greater in honour and in every kind of excellence, was Jesus. He was to be a king, not as Herod supposed, but as it befitted God to give a kingdom, for the good of those who are ruled, to one who would do his subjects no middling or indifferent good, if I may so call it, but would train them and bring them under laws that are truly God's. Jesus knew this; and while he denied that he was a king in the sense in which most people understand it, he taught what sets his own kingdom apart when he said: “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would be fighting, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but as it is, my kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

If Celsus had seen this, he would not have said: “If it was so that you might not grow up and reign in his place, why, now that you have grown up, do you not reign? Why do you, the Son of God, go about begging so ignobly, cowering for fear and wandering wretchedly up and down?”

But it is not ignoble to steer around dangers with deliberate purpose and not rush straight into them, not out of fear of death but so that, by his useful stay in this life, he might help others, until the fitting time should come for the one who had taken on human nature to die a human death, a death that brought something of use to human beings. This is plain to anyone who has understood that Jesus died for human beings; and of this we have spoken, as well as we could, in what came before.

choices.choice: Celsus's Jew is addressing Jesus in the quoted words; Origen here attributes them simply to Celsus ('Celsus ... would not have said'), and the attribution is kept. The opening 'If Herod plotted' presupposes the Jew's charge reported in 1.58 (that Herod killed the infants to destroy Jesus). τὸ χρεών ('what is destined') is rendered without importing a doctrine of fate. 'Killed' and 'in Bethlehem and all its region' quote Matthew 2:16 (ἀνεῖλεν πάντας τοὺς παῖδας τοὺς ἐν Βηθλεὲμ καὶ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῆς); Origen's text lacks πᾶσι and the second ἐν, so the English has 'in its region' (literally 'its borders'), not Matthew's 'in all its region'. Herod's plotting in general recalls Matthew 2:3-8; listed in bible_refs only, as the chapter does not quote it. John 18:36 is quoted with ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου both times and νυνὶ δέ; 'my servants would be fighting' renders ἠγωνίζοντο ἄν. ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς is capitalised as 'the Son of God' because it names Jesus, though in Celsus's mouth it is mockery. ἀγείρεις is taken as 'go about begging' (collecting alms, as a mendicant). μετ᾿ οἰκονομίας is rendered 'with deliberate purpose'. 'In what came before' (ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων) is a cross-reference within this work, probably to the discussion of Jesus' death for humankind earlier in Book 1; not pinned to a chapter here. ἀνομολογουμένην ... συγκατάθεσιν is taken as an assent inconsistent with his belief (the sense found in Aristotle, Rhetoric 2.23), which the following μαχομένας ... κρίσεις ('judgements at war with one another') confirms; rendered 'a conviction at odds with that belief'.
'the Jew in Celsus' changed to 'Celsus's Jew' (same framing, natural English)
συγκατάθεσιν: 'resolve' (a matter of will) changed to 'conviction' (assent of judgement); note added on ἀνομολογουμένην
τὴν ἀκολουθίαν ... τηρῶν: 'keeping watch over the course of events' changed to 'preserving the order of events' (τηρέω here = keep, maintain)

last paragraph: 'spending one's life usefully among them' (switched to a general subject and added 'among them') changed to 'by his useful stay in this life, he might help others', matching αὐτὸν ... ἐπιδημοῦντα
'him who had taken' changed to 'the one who had taken'; 'step aside from' changed to 'steer around' for περιϊστάμενον
